clinicalPearls: A localized bone-remodeling disorder affecting widespread, noncontiguous areas of the skeleton; initiated by overactive osteoclastic resorption followed by compensatory osteoblastic new bone formation, producing a disorganized mosaic of woven and lamellar bone (p.3311).

Most patients are asymptomatic; diagnosis is often made incidentally from an elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) on routine blood chemistry or an abnormal skeletal radiograph obtained for another indication (p.3311, p.3312-3313).
Serum calcium and phosphate levels are normal in Paget's disease; isolated/raised ALP with normal calcium is the characteristic biochemical picture (p.3314).
Sites most commonly involved are the pelvis, vertebral bodies, skull, femur, and tibia; familial early-onset cases often have numerous active sites (p.3313).

The most common presenting symptom is pain, which may arise from increased bony vascularity, expanding lytic lesions, fractures, bowing, or deformity; long-bone bowing causes gait abnormalities and secondary osteoarthritis of hip or knee (p.3313).

Skull involvement may cause headaches, frontal bossing, increased head size, and narrowing of cranial foramina leading to hearing loss (cochlear nerve damage from temporal bone involvement), cranial nerve palsies, and platybasia with risk of brainstem compression (p.3313).

For most patients, serum total ALP remains the test of choice for both diagnosis and assessing response to therapy; bone resorption markers (N-telopeptide, C-telopeptide) fall more rapidly with treatment than ALP (p.3313).
Radionuclide 99mTc bone scans are less specific but more sensitive than standard radiographs for identifying sites of active skeletal lesions (p.3313).
harrison.pathophysiology: The principal abnormality is increased number and activity of osteoclasts, which are large, increased 10- to 100-fold in number, and contain many nuclei (up to 100 vs 3-5 in normal osteoclasts), creating a sevenfold rise in resorptive surfaces. Contributing mechanisms include osteoclast precursor hypersensitivity to 1,25(OH)2D3, hyperresponsiveness to RANK ligand (RANKL), increased RANKL expression by marrow stromal cells, increased IL-6 (raising precursor recruitment), increased c-fos expression, and overexpression of the antiapoptotic oncogene Bcl-2. Osteoblasts are recruited to resorption sites and lay down large amounts of new bone matrix, so turnover is high and bone mass is normal or increased (not reduced) unless there is concomitant calcium/vitamin D deficiency. The process passes through an initial osteolytic phase (prominent resorption and hypervascularization, seen radiographically as an advancing lytic wedge or 'blade of grass' lesion), an active mixed phase replacing lamellar bone with haphazard woven bone (marrow may be replaced by fibrous tissue), and a final sclerotic ('burned-out') phase of hard, dense, less vascular mosaic bone; all three phases may coexist at different sites. Etiology remains unknown but evidence supports both genetic (family history in 15-25%; familial syndromes linked to TNFRSF11B/osteoprotegerin, TNFRSF11A/RANK, profilin 1, valosin-containing protein, and the common SQSTM1/p62 mutation) and viral (paramyxovirus-like inclusions and viral mRNA in osteoclasts) contributions (p.3311-3313).
additionalDifferentials: Osteosarcoma or other sarcoma arising in long-standing pagetic bone (new pain in a long-standing lesion)
Osteoclast-rich benign giant cell tumor arising adjacent to pagetic bone (responds to glucocorticoids)
Metastatic disease in bone (assessed by MRI; definitive diagnosis of malignancy often requires bone biopsy)
Other causes of an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase
nonInfectiousMimics: Familial bone disorders that clinically and radiographically resemble Paget's disease with more severe, earlier-onset presentation: juvenile Paget's disease (familial idiopathic hyperphosphatasia, TNFRSF11B/osteoprotegerin deletion), familial expansile osteolysis, expansile skeletal hyperphosphatasia, and early-onset Paget's disease (TNFRSF11A/RANK mutations)
Inclusion body myopathy with Paget's disease and frontotemporal dementia (IBMPFD; valosin-containing protein mutation)
Sarcoma, giant cell tumor, or metastatic disease producing focal changes in or near pagetic bone
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs (typical findings: bone enlargement/expansion, cortical thickening, coarsened trabeculae, lytic and sclerotic changes; skull 'cotton wool'/osteoporosis circumscripta; 'picture frame' or 'ivory' vertebra; pelvic 'brim sign' and protrusio acetabuli; long-bone bowing)
Radionuclide 99mTc bone scan (more sensitive but less specific than radiographs for active lesions)
Serum total alkaline phosphatase (ALP) - first-line for diagnosis and monitoring; bone-specific ALP may be raised when total ALP is normal in single-site disease
Bone formation marker P1NP (reflects disease activity; can be used instead of total ALP)
Bone resorption markers (serum/urine N-telopeptide or C-telopeptide)
Serum calcium and phosphate (normal in Paget's disease)
CT for assessment of possible fracture; MRI to assess possible sarcoma, giant cell tumor, or metastatic disease
Bone biopsy for definitive diagnosis of suspected malignancy
Note: serum osteocalcin is NOT always elevated and is NOT recommended for diagnosis or management
redFlags: New pain in a long-standing pagetic lesion - suggests sarcomatous (most often osteosarcoma) transformation, although neoplasms arising from pagetic bone are rare (<0.5%)

High-output cardiac state and cardiac enlargement from extensive arteriovenous shunting when large portions (15-35%) of the skeleton are involved with high disease activity (e.g., ALP four times above normal); overt high-output heart failure is relatively rare and usually requires concomitant cardiac pathology
Platybasia (softening of the skull base) with risk of brainstem compression; spinal cord compression from bone enlargement or vascular steal syndrome
Fractures, typically in long bones at areas of active or advancing lytic lesions (common at femoral shaft and subtrochanteric regions)
Discovery of hypercalcemia (even with immobilization) should prompt a search for another cause of hypercalcemia
harrison.prognosis: Most patients are asymptomatic and have a benign course; for unclear reasons the prevalence and severity are decreasing and the age of diagnosis is increasing. Effective potent antiresorptive (bisphosphonate) therapy can normalize bone turnover and is associated with an apparently decreasing incidence of sarcoma. Serious complications - fractures, deformity, secondary osteoarthritis, neurologic compromise (hearing loss, cranial nerve palsies, cord/brainstem compression), high-output cardiac state, and rare (<0.5%) malignant transformation (usually osteosarcoma) - drive morbidity. Whether early therapy prevents late complications remains to be determined; deformities may take many years to manifest (p.3312-3314).
pitfalls: Assuming an isolated raised ALP is benign - it can be the only clue to asymptomatic Paget's disease and warrants workup (radiograph plus bone scan).
A symptomatic patient with progression at a single site may have a normal total ALP but an increased bone-specific ALP.
Using serum osteocalcin to diagnose or monitor disease - it is not always elevated and is not recommended.
Attributing hypercalcemia to Paget's disease/immobilization - normal calcium and phosphate are expected, so hypercalcemia should prompt a search for another cause.

Starting bisphosphonate therapy without ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake first - very active bone formation with rapid resorption suppression can precipitate hypocalcemia or mild secondary hyperparathyroidism.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a formal staging system. Disease activity is gauged by the extent of skeletal involvement and the degree of bone-turnover marker elevation (notably total ALP, with ALP roughly four times above normal cited as marking high activity and cardiovascular risk when 15-35% of the skeleton is involved). Pathologically the disease evolves through three phases that may coexist: an osteolytic phase, an active mixed (woven-bone) phase, and a final sclerotic 'burned-out' phase (p.3313-3314).
management: Normalise the accelerated bone turnover with a potent bisphosphonate, intravenous zoledronic acid being first-line, or an oral aminobisphosphonate such as risedronate
Ensure calcium and vitamin D repletion before intravenous bisphosphonate to avoid hypocalcaemia
Control bone pain with analgesia, recognising that much pain also responds to antiresorptive therapy
Monitor disease activity and treatment response with total or bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, or P1NP
Involve orthopaedics for pathological fracture, progressive deformity, secondary osteoarthritis needing joint replacement, or impending long-bone bowing
Surveil for complications including hearing loss and cranial neuropathies from skull involvement, spinal stenosis, and rare sarcomatous transformation signalled by new pain or a mass
Manage within a metabolic bone service with audiology and neurosurgical input as complications dictate
